verses.text: Let us begin our song with the Muses of Helicon,
who live on Helicon, the great and sacred mountain,
and on soft feet, around the violet-dark spring
and the altar of mighty Zeus, son of Cronus, they dance.
After washing their tender skin in the waters of Permessus,
or the Horse’s Spring, or the sacred river Olmeius,
they form their dances on the highest slopes of Helicon,
beautiful, lovely dances, their feet moving with vigor.
From there the Muses set out, wrapped in thick mist,
walking through the night, their beautiful voices rising,
singing of Zeus, who bears the aegis shield, and majestic Hera
of Argos, who walks in golden sandals;
of bright-eyed Athena, daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis;
of shining Apollo and Artemis, who showers arrows;
of Poseidon, who holds the earth and shakes it;
of honored Themis and Aphrodite with her curling lashes;
of Hebe crowned in gold and beautiful Dione;
of Leto and Iapetus, and Cronus with his crooked schemes;
of Eos the Dawn, great Helios the Sun, and bright Selene the Moon;
of Gaia the Earth, great Oceanus, and black Night;
and of the sacred family of all the other gods who live forever.
These Muses once taught Hesiod beautiful song
as he tended lambs below sacred Helicon.
These were the first words the goddesses spoke to me,
the Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who bears the aegis:
“Shepherds who live in the fields, shameful creatures, nothing but bellies!
We know how to tell many lies that sound like the truth;
we also know, when we choose, how to speak the truth.”
So spoke great Zeus’s daughters, sure and skillful with words.
They gave me a staff, a branch of flourishing laurel
they had plucked, a wondrous sight, and breathed into me a voice
divine, so I could sing of things to come and things long past.
They told me to praise the family of blessed gods who live forever,
and always to sing of the Muses themselves, first and last.
But why all this talk of oak or rock?
Come, let us begin with the Muses, who sing to their father Zeus
and delight his mighty mind within Olympus,
telling of what is, what will be, and what was before,
their voices joining as one. Their tireless song flows
sweetly from their mouths, and their father’s halls laugh,
the halls of thundering Zeus, as the goddesses’ lily-like voices
spread. The peak of snowy Olympus echoes,
and so do the homes of the immortal gods. Raising their deathless voices,
the Muses first praise in song the honored family of gods
from the beginning, those born to Gaia the Earth and wide Uranus the Sky,
and the gods descended from them, the givers of good things.
Next they sing of Zeus, father of gods and humans,
both as they begin their song and as they bring it to an end,
telling how far he surpasses the gods, how greatest he is in power.
Then, singing of the human race and the mighty Giants,
they delight Zeus’s mind within Olympus,
the Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who bears the aegis.

uncertainties: The reference to “oak or rock” in verse 35 is obscure; the literal image is retained.
The description of the voices as “lily-like” in verse 41 may suggest delicacy or purity; its exact force is uncertain.
